title: Why Do You Dream 2 Hours Every Night? 💤
description:

topic: Why do we dream? (~2 h of dreaming a night, vivid dreams in REM; amygdala active while prefrontal logic areas quiet down, so odd dreams feel normal; Stickgold 2000 Tetris study: most players, even some amnesic patients who couldn't remember playing, saw falling blocks at sleep onset; sleep may replay the day to consolidate memory)
script: Your brain makes two hours of movies every night. So why does it even bother? Most vivid dreams happen in REM sleep, when your eyes dart around under your eyelids. Your brain's emotion center fires up, while the part that checks logic goes quiet. That's why riding a giant cat to school feels totally normal. Now the weird part. In 2000, Harvard scientists had people play Tetris for three days. At night, most saw falling blocks as they drifted off. Even some patients with amnesia, who couldn't remember playing at all. Scientists think sleep may replay your day to save it. So what did your brain replay last night?
key_facts: Most people dream about 2 hours per night across several REM cycles (Sleep Foundation: How Long Do Dreams Last?)

The most vivid dreams happen in REM (rapid eye movement) sleep; emotional/limbic areas such as the amygdala are highly active while prefrontal areas tied to logic are less active, which helps explain bizarre dreams feeling normal (Wikipedia: REM sleep; PsyPost neuroscience of dreaming)

Stickgold et al., Science 2000 (Harvard Medical School): after playing Tetris over 3 days, 17 of 27 participants reported Tetris images as they fell asleep, including 3 of 5 amnesic patients who could not remember playing (Science 290:350; Harvard Gazette)
Memory consolidation is a leading (not proven) theory of why we dream; hedged as 'scientists think ... may' in the script
